RE: LD1020- An Act Repealing the Laws of the Gorham Connector
Dear Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and Honorable Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Transportation,
Founded in 1964, Greater Portland Landmarks is a non-profit advocacy organization that works toward the preservation and revitalization of greater Portland's built environment. Our goal is to save greater Portland's historic places through preservation and adaptive use while promoting creative new architecture that enhances historic neighborhoods. We appreciate the opportunity to comment in support of LD1010- An Act Repealing the Laws of the Gorham Connector.
As proposed, the highway connecting South Portland and Gorham will dissect one of the country's oldest family-run farms: Smiling Hill Farm in Westbrook/Scarborough. Found eligible for the National Register of Historic Places, this farm was established c. 1720 by Colonel Thomas Westbrook and his nephew Nathaniel Knight. Many of the structures are over a century old, and the farm functions much as it has for generations. The highway would decimate the hay fields that support the diary functions of the farm and would likely destroy the remaining operations by default. Maine's historic farms and open spaces are increasingly threatened by sprawl and unimaginative transportation solutions like the Gorham Connector.
Greater Portland Landmarks supports this bill and strongly urges all involved to collaborate towards more sensible traffic solutions that support our irreplaceable historic resources instead of destroying them. We are happy to partner towards that end.
Sincerely,
Kate Lemos McHale Executive Director
Greater Portland Landmarks' mission is to ensure that Greater Portland preserves its sense of place for all and builds vibrant, sustainable neighborhoods and communities for the future.

Testimony of Amelia Neilson In Support of LD 1020
April 3, 2025
Dear Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and Honorable Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Transportation,
My name is Amelia Neilson, I live in Bath, and I am an active advocate around bicycle, pedestrian, and public transportation issues in my town. I also know from living Bath that high traffic roads, even on a small scale, can significantly segregate a town - North and South Bath may as well be separate towns for as frequently as there's crossover under the Route 1 overpass.
I support LD 1020 because:  Back when this law was passed to allow the MTA to build the Connector, the MTA estimated far more traffic on these roads by 2025 than we have actually seen. They were wrong then, and they will be wrong again. Furthermore, history has shown time and time again that increasing road capacity and building additional car infrastructure does not address traffic issues: it only incentivizes more car use and therefore cannot stop congestion.  MTA does not control where people live and work, commuter and tourist frequency, or where development of stores, schools, and industries occurs. As mentioned above, they have already failed to accurately predict traffic. This project is a waste of time and money that locks us into unnecessary infrastructure. The money would be better spent on projects that coincide with smart, sustainable development of the Greater Portland area and that align with a vision for increased public transportation, community connection, and mixed use areas. The metro area is changing; we cannot lean into inflexible options like the proposed connector that will not only not address future development needs but in fact hinder them.  To put some numbers on the connector: the MTA's own studies said a highway would make a tiny difference in commute times, perhaps 4 minutes on average. A $330 million minimum price tag is too much for such a small effect.  Finally, towns like Scarborough and Westbrook have argued against the connector, as have advocates who point out that it would decimate Smiling Hill Farm - a heritage dairy farm and community staple. Why would we not listen to community member wants and needs?
Thank you for your time and attention. I hope the committee sees the reason in repealing the Gorham Connector project.
Amelia Neilson

Andrea Giddings Scarborough LD 1020
I am writing to express opposition to the Gorham Connector.
As a resident of North Scarborough, I commute daily along Rt 22 and Rt 114 to my job as a teacher at the Scarborough Middle School. Contrary to claims, the traffic congestion on these routes is not excessively severe. While congestion may occur during specific times, such as rush hours, it is typically brief and does not warrant the drastic measure of constructing a new 4-lane toll highway.
Instead of rushing into such a costly and destructive massive infrastructure project like the Gorham Connector, we should first prioritize exploring and implementing alternative solutions to address the traffic issues, like improving our existing roads. More efficient intersections like roundabouts in the current areas of congestion would go a long way to relieving backed up traffic on Rt 114 and Rt 22. Perhaps most importantly, building paved shoulders on Rt 114, Rt 22, and other local roads like Running Hill, would finally give us North Scarborough residents the ability to safely bike and run and walk along these roads and not have to take our cars everywhere.
In the long term, developing public transit and complimentary land use changes, as outlined in the 2012 Gorham East-West Corridor study, will further aid in reducing traffic. The lack of implementation of the 2012 study recommendations is concerning. Before committing to such a large-scale and destructive infrastructure project as the Gorham Connector, it is essential that we explore and implement the other recommendations laid out in the study to address traffic issues effectively.
I really want to see this community thrive and would love the option of biking or running to work, or hopping on a bus to downtown Portland. I urge the state to reconsider its support for the Gorham Connector turnpike project that will destroy our community instead. Let's concentrate on prioritizing investments in alternative transportation methods that truly benefit our community. Investing in road shoulders for bike and pedestrian use, bus services, and other sustainable transit options will not only reduce congestion and improve mobility but also enhance the overall livability and sustainability of our community.
Thank you for considering my perspective on this matter.

Perhaps one must let go of a stanza in a poem that one has been working on for some time, it could mean cutting whole pages out of a story, and even deleting multiple chapters from a book- chapters that one might have spent, hours, weeks, months, even years working on. Killing your darlings is tough work-you have grown attached to your darlings for good reason, because when you have worked on something for a long time you, come to love it. Abandoning them can feel like abandoning a part of yourself. But something miraculous happens when you are willing to let go of these words, these chapters, these projects that have become useless or antiquated within the writing-you make space for new, creative endeavors within the work. Once the writer is able to let go of what is no longer serving the work as whole, the writing project begins to thrive in a new and unprecedented way. It takes a lot strength, resiliency and wisdom to have the courage to abandon your darlings. I speak from experience when I tell you that-when you are brave enough and wise enough to kill your darlings, the possibilities within the work become endless.
Thank you for your consideration, for representing the People, and for your service to our state.

Julie Larry Biddeford LD 1020
I support the passage of LD1020 to repeal the Maine Turnpike authority to expand the turnpike to include what is known as the Gorham Connector. The connector would bulldoze through the fields of Smiling Hill Farm, a significant recreational, agricultural, and historic farm in Westbrook, Gorham, and Scarborough.
The Maine Historic Preservation Commission has formally determined the farm to be eligible for the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) which provides it with the same level of protections as if it were on the NRHP. This would include the whole farm property, not just the buildings, as the woodlands and fields historically associated with the operation of the farm contribute to the farm's historic significance.
A determination of eligibility does not place any burden on the property owner, but it does offer some protection when projects undertaken by a federal agency, using federal funding, or needing a federal permit will impact that historic resource. I understand that the Maine Turnpike Authority has been in conversation with the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and likely needs a USACE permit for the project, triggering an assessment of the impact the proposed connector will have on the farm.
Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966, as amended, requires Federal agencies to take into account the effects of their undertakings on Historic Properties. Therefore, prior to the issuance or authorization of any permit under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act, Section 10 of the Rivers and Harbors Act of 1899, Section 103 of the Marine Protection, Research and Sanctuaries Act of 1972, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers must consider the effect the authorization may have on Historic Properties.
In the last thirty years I have worked on numerous projects as an architectural historian assessing project impacts for the telecommunications, energy, and transportation sectors. In my opinion the proposed connector would have significant adverse visual and physical impacts on Smiling Hill Farm. If LD 1020 can help to provide transportation alternatives to solve the traffic problem on Routes 22/114, then I urge you to support its passage.

Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, Members of the Transportation Committee, My name is Roberta Manter, I live in Fayette, and I am asking you to support LD 1020.
The MTA believed there was "silent majority" that supported this project. If so, why didn't they show up at the hearings? I submit that the true silent majority consists of those who could not travel an hour and a half or more each way to Gorham to express their opposition to the connector. I am here to speak for them. This is not just a "not in my back yard" situation. Smiling Hill Farm is a state treasure, and they share it generously. Their influence stretches far and wide - I contend, much wider than the area that allegedly would benefit from the Connector.
Farms generally operate close to the edge. That's why in addition to farming they seek as many other sources of income as they can - maple sugaring, lumber, petting zoo, tour groups, cross country skiing, ski equipment rentals, etc. Farms depend on acreage to survive, and that acreage has to be readily accessible. ANYTHING that makes it harder on a farm can be the straw that breaks the camel's back. We are losing farms at an alarming rate, especially dairy farms.
Smiling Hill Farm supplies fresh dairy products to stores as far away as Lewiston, Augusta, and Waterville. And people who come here to cross country ski, come from all over the United States. Maine depends heavily on tourism. People don't come to Maine to travel our highways, they come to Maine to see our unspoiled countryside. When a farm can no longer sustain itself, it may be sold for development, or a solar farm, and we lose all that scenic beauty and open space. If you eliminate Smiling Hill Farm, where will people from Portland go to see a farm? And once our farms are gone, WHAT WILL WE EAT? We need our farms, and we need to do everything within our power to see that the few farms we have left remain sustainable.
Each year, Smiling Hill Farm hosts hundreds of tour groups - schools, homeschool groups, the children who will shape our future. Many travel over an hour and a half to get there. How many thousands of children have benefited, over the years this program has been offered? How many of them got to learn the importance of our farms, and will support them in the future, or perhaps even go into farming themselves?
Years ago I helped take a variety of animals to a "Farm Day" in New York City's Central Park. It was a unique one-day opportunity for city kids to see and touch farm animals. As we were leaving the city with our menagerie in a slat-sided stock trailer, we got stopped at a traffic light. A father happened to be walking by with his young son, and suddenly saw the opportunity he had missed. He picked up the boy and literally ran the length of the trailer, saying, "Horse! Cow! Donkey! Sheep! Goat! Pig!" Then the light changed, and we had to drive on. Is that what we want for our children in Maine? Smiling Hill Farm is here 365 days a year, not for a few seconds at a traffic light.
Again, this isn't just "not in my back yard," this is something that affects people far and wide. There are few spots they could have chosen that would have wider consequences than to damage Smiling Hill Farm. Please, count the cost.

Testimony of Stanis Moody-Roberts
In Support Of
LD 1020, An Act to Repeal the Laws Providing for the Construction of a Connector to Gorham
April 3rd, 2025
Sen. Nangle, Rep. Crafts, and Distinguished Members of the Transportation Committee,
My name is Stanis Moody-Roberts, and I live with my family in North Scarborough, across from Smiling Hill Farm. Like Smiling Hill and many other neighbors, my home, and my life, is also in
the path of the MTA's proposed Gorham Connector turnpike highway. I speak to you today to urge your support of LD 1020, An Act to Repeal the Laws Providing for the Construction of a
Connector to Gorham. The MTA has been deeply dishonest, adversarial, and condescending in
its efforts to push this destructive project through over the widespread opposition in our community. It is telling that our entire legislative delegation, as well as the town councils of Scarborough and Westbrook, have taken action to oppose this project that would be so harmful
to South Gorham and North Scarborough residents.
Picture the things that you love most in this world, that you would sacrifice everything in order to protect. Perhaps it is your husband or wife, your soulmate, your parents or your children.
For me it is all those things, but it is also my home. I am lucky to live in a most beautiful corner of this world, a house on a small pond nestled in the woods, that I built myself with my bare hands. For close to a decade, I juggled multiple jobs, lived out of my car, lived covertly out of my office, and then lived in a shipping container with no electricity or running water through two Maine winters in order to build this dream. It is where I met the love of my life, where I raise my chickens and my bees, where Ijust had my first child, and where I will grow old and gray if the MTA does not pave me over first.
Eminent domain, the forced governmental seizure of people's homes and property, is an act of violence. It may be legal, and perhaps it can be justified for the "greater good", but it is a
heartbreaking, gut-wrenching concept that utterly destroys the lives that are victim to it. It should only ever be considered as a last possible resort, after everything else with less impact
has been tried and an overwhelming majority of a community is demanding it.
The Gorham Connector would destroy my home that I love and hold dear, along with the homes of so many other of my neighbors here in North Scarborough. It would destroy our
beloved Smiling Hill Farm, one of the oldest generational farms in this country, that the Knight

Family has stewarded for over 300 years and has brought such delight to generations of children growing up in Greater Portland. lt would entail paving over around 40 acres of protected
wetlands, polluting and severely impairing the headwaters of Red Brook, and bisect so many acres of undeveloped wildlife habitat that make our community the beautiful place that it is subjecting our community to the resulting highway pollution, noise pollution, runoff, clearcutting, re-grading and drainage basin disruption that constructing a new four-lane divided highway entails. According to the MTA's 2023 cost update, it would cost our state $650 million to construct and maintain over just the first 30 years -- close to $1 billion when factoring in the bond interest -- money that while perhaps being paid for through tolls, would still be coming out
of the pockets of hardworking Mainers that should not have to be subject to yet another cost-
of-living increase.
Traffic all along this corridor is significantly below what it was twenty years ago (and was down
even in 2019 pre-covid), which is remarkable considering that the region has grown by around
20% during that time. That data is not just anecdotal -- it is statistically borne out through ME DOT historical traffic counts. It is true on Rt 25, on Rt 22, on Rt 114, on New Portland Rd, and
on Running Hill Rd.
There are far less costly and far less destructive ways of alleviating traffic congestion along this
corridor. Our MPO, PACTS, considers a two-lane state highway over capacity if either its AADT is above 18,000 or if its peak hour is above 1950 VPH. The only place along the Rt 25/ Rt 114/ Rt 22 corridor west of Portland where that is true is the 1-mile Rt 22/ Rt 114 overlap section.
Intersection improvements, and limited widening of this one short bottleneck, would go such a long way towards alleviating the congestion in this area, as envisioned by the 1997 GorhamPortland Alternatives Analysis, the 1999 Route 22/114 Location Study, the 2002 PACTS 22/114 Overlap Study, Scarborough's 2003 Transportation Plan, and the PACTS 2003 Destination
Tomorrow plan. Yet ever since the MTA became the lead agency for solving traffic congestion in
this area two decades ago, nothing has been done to try to improve our existing roads, as the
MTA can only do one thing -- build a new four-lane limited access toll highway.
Revoking the MTA's authorization to build the Gorham Connector would finally allow for all
other alternatives to be fairly considered. It does not prevent the MTA from coming back to the
legislature someday with a new, more community-centered proposal, if they are able to
somehow able to regain our community's trust and support in the future. But it does ensure that any future MTA proposal must go through a democratic process -- and be approved by the
legislature -- before ever moving forward. That is never a bad thing.
With appreciation for your time and consideration,
Stanis Moody-Roberts
